catalog_quote: p. 6: "Some notable features in the phonology of Yintyingka are found in the phoneme inventory, in phonotactic patterns, and especially in the system of word stress. ... Stems in Yintyingka are almost exclusively vowel-final, and a bit over ten percent of stems are vowel-initial, historically derived from the dropping of initial consonants. ... The location of word stress depends primarily on the size of the word, with stress on the first syllable for bisyllabic words and the second syllable for trisyllabic words, and secondarily on the presence of an initial vowel, with stress on the second syllable for bisyllabic words beginning with a short vowel. Word stress influences a whole range of allophonic processes around the edges of the second syllable in the word, like consonant gemination, optional vowel lengthening and voicing of stops." p. 87 (Google Books snippet): "... size of the word: trisyllabic words have stress on the second syllable, while bisyllabic words usually have stress on the first syllable. A secondary parameter that plays a minor role is the distinction between consonant-initial and vowel-initial stems: bisyllabic stems beginning ..." p. 90 (snippet): "... secondary stress on the third. This is illustrated in Figure 7 below, where pikipiki shows the major fall on the first syllable, and a new fall on the third syllable (in this token, the last syllable does not continue the fall ..."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable but not tied to one fixed edge position: disyllabic words are stressed on the first syllable, trisyllabic words on the second syllable; disyllabic words that begin with a short vowel (historically initial-dropped stems) shift stress to the second syllable. Established instrumentally (pitch and amplitude, Praat/Winpitch) on elicited single words from archival recordings, and corroborated by stress-conditioned segmental effects (consonant gemination, optional vowel lengthening, stop voicing around the second syllable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.90 (snippet): a four-syllable token pikipiki 'shows the major fall on the first syllable, and a new fall on the third syllable', described as secondary stress on the third syllable; index lists 'primary vs secondary stress 90-92'. Full treatment of 4+-syllable words not read.
new_statements.exceptions: Bisyllabic words 'usually' initial (p.87); vowel-initial bisyllabic stems with a short initial vowel take second-syllable stress (p.6, 87); certain enclitics (e.g. =nhang, p.118) attract stress / shift stress toward the second syllable ('stress attraction' 87, 92, 117, 118 in index); in phrases, stress falls consistently on the first syllable of the second word, which conflicts with the trisyllabic word pattern, so the authors separate word stress from phrase stress (pp.96-97).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is explicitly about word stress in words elicited in isolation (single words or short phrases from archival sound recordings, p.86); sec. 5.3 treats phrase stress separately (first syllable of the second word in two-word phrases). Language no longer spoken; analysis from 1920s-1990s archival material.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Yintyingka (the coastal Princess Charlotte Bay language, reconstructed from 1920s-1990s archival recordings; authors place it in Eastern Middle Paman with Umpithamu and Umpila). Glottolog 5.1 languoid ayab1239 'Yintyinka-Ayabadhu' (ISO ayd) lists this grammar as its only descriptive reference, so identity is direct. Note the name Ayapathu/Ayabadhu is also used in the literature for an inland Wik-affiliated variety ('Western Ayapathu'), which is a different language and is not what this grammar describes; the book's index has an entry 'Yintyingka (people) - relations with Ayapathu people'.

tone.quote: The basic diagnostic criterion for word stress in Umpithamu is that primary stress is the (potential) location of the primary pitch movement in the utterance, which in lexical elication coincides with the word. As in many cases, there is no study of native speaker judgements to confirm this, but this is the way word stress has been diagnosed in many Australian languages (see Fletcher & Butcher 2014), including in the region (e.g. Verstraete & Rigsby 2015); as will be discussed below there is also segmental evidence supporting this analysis.
